p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for more than ten months, and the countdown clock says 447.
This fall the program made an uncrewed path through the window a declared option: the autonomy release is being built so the ship could fly the Breather to Mars and land it if the crew can't go.
A code assistant slipped Earth's gravity into a Mars landing routine, and the integrated sim caught it.

AR 2207 is still open, with the second test article's life test still running clean, and on the station Malik, the son of Frances Odum, who speaks for the colonists' families, has a cough that won't go away.
Now Nell Garrity of Aldergrove, the valve's maker, has asked to be paid for root cause work beyond what the fixed price contract covers, and Garrett wants them fired.
Peg Sato. Tallgrass contracts and procurement.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Nell Garrity. Aldergrove's account lead, the "valve lady." She brought her company's Petrel records, carried for twenty six years.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Paloma Benavidez. Test engineer at Rio Puerco Electrochemical in Albuquerque, the only person who has run the Breather's stacks at Mars pressure.

Same Monday, fifteen minutes later. November 28, 2061, 8:20 AM. Peg Sato, who read fine print for fun, had brought two coffees into Sam's office and drunk both of them while he read, and she was looking at the empty second cup as if it had let her down.

Aldergrove's letter of November 23, 2061, on the valve contract. One: since April 29 they've put 4,800 engineering hours into the AR 2207 investigation at the program's request, and clause 14 covers 600 a contract year at no added cost. Two: they ask for an equitable adjustment of $1,008,000 for the 4,200 hours over that, at their audited rate. Three: the rest of the root cause work can't be priced, since nobody knows what it'll find, so they ask to move it out of the fixed price into a separate cost reimbursable task order, estimated at $4.6 million through the stage's shipment. Four: they'll keep working while it's considered. N. Garrity, account lead.

Under the letter, clipped at the corner, was the photocopy. A page of rev C cold cycle data from 2034, columns of temperatures and closing times gone soft and gray the way a copy of a copy goes. Somebody in 2034 had drawn a box around the third row in pencil. The copier had caught half of a note in the margin beside it, in a slanted hand, CYCLE 3 AFTER SO, and the rest had fallen off the edge of the glass, all but a single initial under it, W. Beside the third row, in blue ink, in the same hand as the signature on the letter: Still asking.

It's a request for equitable adjustment, Peg said. Which is the polite way to start a claim. Nobody's sued anybody. Nobody's stopped work. Paragraph four says they'll keep going while we think about it, which they didn't have to say, and which I'd like framed.

Garrett had called her at six that morning. She'd written down what he said on the back of an envelope, and she turned it around so Sam could read it. They're holding our valve hostage. Find me another supplier by Friday. I'll make the calls.

Sam read the letter a third time. The 600 hours in clause 14 had been written in 2058 by somebody who'd pictured a supplier answering a few questions on the phone, a week of an engineer's time, maybe two. Aldergrove had given the program eight times that since April, and as far as Sam knew every hour of it had gone into finding out whether a valve was going to hurt four people on their way to Mars.

Quinn knocked on the open door with the integrated plan rolled under her arm. She unrolled the departure stage's line across his desk and held the corners down with his stapler and Peg's empty cups. The stage was due to ship to the Cape in July. The valve in the letter had been inside it since September 2059. Whatever we do, she said, it happens in front of that.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 447.
Garrett wants a new supplier by Friday. The Administrator said the same thing to me once, about the same company.

57 days before launch. oh seven hundred, Garrity, Aldergrove, on the line. wants to hold the last flight valve 3 weeks and run the shelf valve cold in Pueblo. 500 cycles. Wendell's number. it was in our october risk board minutes. asks for a change order to pay for it. oh seven fifteen, contracts: firm fixed price. delivery April 30. a hold is late delivery. oh seven forty, administrator: if the valve isn't here on the 30TH we terminate for default and buy from somebody who ships. oh seven forty five, nobody else ships a 7740. everybody on the line knew it. nobody said it. me either. oh eight ten, called Garrity back. told him we need it on the 30TH. he asked if i'd looked at his row 3. told him i'd looked at the schedule. oh eight eleven, that was true. April 30 1400 valve received on time. cover letter: shipped under protest. we are still asking about cycle 3. E. Garrity. April 30 1430 filed the letter with the receiving papers.

Tuesday, November 29. 7:30 AM. Peg had spent the evening with the contract, all two hundred and twelve pages of it, and had come in with eleven sticky flags along its edge in four colors, which she said was a system.

The life test on the second test article had been extended twice and was past six thousand cold cycles in Building 6, all of them clean, which Wendell said had taught them a great deal about what the cause wasn't. Aldergrove's engineers were at the console beside him most nights. Either way, nobody on the team said soon anymore.

Clause 14 is six hundred hours a year, Peg said. Whatever paper anybody signed in the spring, none of it says four thousand eight hundred. And here's the part Garrett won't like. We asked for those hours. Hana's team sent them work orders. Some of the work orders have your initials on them.

Garrett had already called legal. Legal had a two paragraph reply drafted by nine: the contract is firm fixed price, clause 14 is the limit, the request is denied. Hana had read it over Peg's shoulder and put it down on the table face first. If their people walk, half my root cause team walks with them. They're the only engineers alive who've built a 7740.

Peg logs it in the contract file as CL-0012 and writes to Aldergrove for the hour records, by work order. Sam calls Pueblo at noon. Nell Garrity, Aldergrove's account lead, answers on the first ring, which he notices. Thank you for calling instead of writing. She tells him the past hours matter less to her than the next six months. I can't give you a fixed price for finding out something nobody knows. If I make one up, I'm either robbing you or I'm going to stop looking when the money runs out. I won't do either one. By Friday Peg has the count. Thirty six hundred of the hours tie to work orders the program wrote. Six hundred were Aldergrove scanning its own archive, which helped everybody, and which Aldergrove had decided to do on its own.

Claims administration starts with treating the claim as what it is, a request under the contract that deserves a review. Document it, verify its basis against your own records, keep the work going, and talk to the person behind the letter before the positions harden.
Thursday, December 1. 7:00 AM. Garrett was in the big room before anyone else, with a single page on the table and his reading glasses on top of it.
KESTREL FLOW CONTROLS COLORADO SPRINGS LETTER OF INTEREST. KESTREL CAN DELIVER A QUALIFIED CRYOGENIC ISOLATION VALVE FOR THE HALCYON DEPARTURE STAGE BY MAY 2062. FIRM FIXED PRICE. WE DON'T DO CLAIMS.
Garrett had heard about the claim on Monday and had been making calls ever since, as he'd said he would.
Fixed price, he said, tapping the page. No claims. They're hungry and they're an hour and a half down the road. Terminate Aldergrove, Peg drafts it today, and we're done being held hostage.
Hana read the page twice. Qualified to what? How many times has a Kestrel valve closed after a cold soak at this size? I'll tell you. None. Ours is already in the stage.

Peg didn't say anything in the meeting. Afterward she came to Sam's office with a printout from the state's business filings. Kestrel's board chair was a man who also sat on Tallgrass's investor board, which had met on November 15. Garrett hadn't mentioned it.

Quinn and Hana have the comparison by four. Kestrel's valve has never closed cold at this size. Replacing the installed valve means destacking, a new qualification of at least seven months, and a second acceptance firing, and the stage misses its slot at the Cape and the window behind it. Peg adds the contract side: Aldergrove isn't in default, and a wrongful default becomes a termination for convenience, so the program would pay Aldergrove's costs and lose its engineers too. Sam writes it into the risk register as R-0517, claim unresolved with the sole qualified supplier, response mitigate, by negotiation. At the bottom of the page is one more line: Kestrel's board chair sits on Tallgrass's investor board. Sam sends it to Garrett first, alone. Garrett calls him in eleven minutes. You think I'd put a valve on a ship for a friend? No, sir, Sam says. I think the change board should know, so nobody else has to wonder. A long pause. Fine. Put it in. On Wednesday the board records it with a mitigation: any decision involving Kestrel comes to the board without Garrett's vote, and Garrett agrees.

Assess a supplier switch as a risk decision, with data: qualification, schedule, and the people who know the part. Termination needs grounds and has consequences. A link between a decision maker and a bidder is a conflict of interest to disclose, whoever holds it.
Monday, December 5. Peg had divided the big room whiteboard down the middle with a line of blue tape. On the left, in her capitals, WHAT WE KNOW. On the right, WHAT WE DON'T.

The left side was short. The valve was a 7740 rev F. It had one real event on record, 40 milliseconds, the third close after a cold soak. A second test article had cycled six thousand times without doing it again. The right side ran down to the floor. Why. How many cycles. Whether the answer needed a teardown. Whether there would be a fix, and what it would cost, and who would build it.

Aldergrove's estimate for the remaining work was $4.6 million, and Nell had said on the phone that $0.6 million of it was Aldergrove's own contingency, because a supplier quoting the unknowable pads the quote.

Peg had three drafts on the table, a fixed price, time and materials with a cap, and cost plus incentive fee. Garrett's assistant had forwarded a fourth that morning: cost plus award fee, with the award decided each quarter by the office of the CEO.

Hana stood at the right side of the board with a marker she hadn't used yet. Whatever we sign, she said, has to pay them to find the answer. It can't pay them to stop looking, and it can't pay them to look forever.

Peg drafts it at the table and Nell redlines it by phone the same afternoon. Target cost $4.0 million, which is Aldergrove's estimate with its own contingency taken out, because a cost type contract doesn't need it. Target fee eight percent, $320,000. Share 80/20, buyer first. Minimum fee $120,000, maximum $520,000. Deliverables by the month: a data package to the root cause team, a status to the board's clerk, and, when there is one, a root cause report. Peg checks the one thing the rules say to check first. Aldergrove's accounting system was audited for cost type work in 2059, and it passed. Hana reads the draft and finally uses her marker, on the right side of the board, under WHY. It pays them to look efficiently, she says. It doesn't pay them to stop.

When the scope can't be defined, a cost reimbursable contract fits, and an incentive fee gives the seller a reason to control cost. Define the deliverables and the fee formula up front, and confirm the seller can account for costs before you sign.

Wednesday, December 7. The program's change board met at two, as it did every Wednesday, in the big room with the integrated plan on the wall and a plate of somebody's cookies going stale in the middle of the table.

The first item on the agenda was Aldergrove: settle the past hours, and move the remaining root cause work out of the fixed price into a separate task order, cost plus incentive fee, as drafted on Monday.

At 1:40 Garrett called Peg directly. You've got signing authority to ten million. Sign it. I don't need a committee looking at my supplier. Peg had the authority. She'd been given it in writing in 2057 and had it framed, next to a drawing her nephew had made of a dragon.
She came to the board anyway, with the modification in a folder, and sat down beside Sam. I can sign this, she said quietly. The question is whether I should yet.

CR-0388 goes up at two. What changes in the contract. Where the money comes from: contingency, from the line AR 2207 has had since June. What it does to the root cause schedule and to the stage's ship date, which is nothing, if the work keeps going. What it does to the risk register: R-0517 down a notch, a new one for a cost type contract the program has never managed before. The board approves the structure, sets the limits Sam and Peg will carry into the negotiation, and records the decision with the reasons. Quinn updates the plan before the cookies are gone. Peg puts the unsigned modification back in her folder. After Pueblo, she says. Then it'll mean something.

A contract change is a project change. Assess its effect on cost, schedule, scope, and risk through integrated change control and record the decision, and then the person with contracting authority signs it and the documents get updated.
Friday, December 9. The meeting was set for Wednesday the 14th, at ten, at Aldergrove's plant on the south side of Pueblo. Aldergrove would bring its president, Nell, and its lawyer.

Garrett wanted to lead it. CEO to CEO. They'll want to see the man who signs. Tallgrass's legal office wanted to send two lawyers and keep it formal. Hana had already cleared the day. Gwen Talley, Hale's chief of staff, had called to ask, carefully, whether the ARA should know anything before Wednesday, since the ARA would be the one explaining any of it to the board and the partners.
Peg had made a list of who could go and what each of them would change by being in the room. She'd written GARRETT at the top and then, beside it in smaller letters, phone.

Garrett signs the limits on Monday morning after Peg walks him through the work orders: up to $1.0 million on the past hours, and the task order as the board approved it. He agrees to be on his phone in Denver at 10:30 for a check in. Sam calls Gwen that afternoon with what the program is going to ask for, why, and what it would mean for the board's AR 2207 data, which is that the board would get more of it. The Director likes hearing it before rather than after, she says. Tell us how it ends, the same day. Hana spends the weekend making a single page of what the root cause team needs from Aldergrove through the summer, in order.

Engaging stakeholders means deciding who participates, in what role, and with what authority, and keeping the people affected informed. Put the person who knows the contract at the table with written limits, keep the decision maker reachable, and brief the sponsor before the meeting.
Monday, December 12. Peg ran the prep session in the big room with the door shut: Sam, Hana, Quinn, and a yellow legal pad she'd divided into columns with a ruler.

The first column was POSITIONS. Aldergrove: $1,008,000 for the past hours, and a cost type contract for the rest. Tallgrass legal: nothing for the past hours, and the fixed price stands. She read them both out and then drew a line under them.

Those are positions, she said. I don't negotiate positions. I negotiate what's under them. If we go down there and trade numbers, we'll end up halfway between two numbers nobody believes, and we'll all feel very grown up about it.
Garrett's text arrived at 10:15, to Peg and Sam. Open at 200K. Tell them Kestrel is ready. It works.
Peg turned the pad to a clean page.

The pad fills up. Aldergrove's interests: being paid for work done, a contract that doesn't punish it for finding the answer, cash in March for sixty people, and the truth about cycle 3. Tallgrass's: the root cause before the stage ships, cost it can explain to an auditor, and Aldergrove's engineers still at the table in June. Then the alternatives, with numbers, which Quinn checks twice. If there's no deal, the claim goes to arbitration; Peg's estimate of what that would cost Tallgrass, and of what it would net Aldergrove, gives each side's walk away point and a wide zone between them. Then the standard: the program's own work orders. Thirty six hundred hours at Aldergrove's audited rate is $864,000. It sits inside the zone. Nobody has to win that number, she says. It's ours, and it's true. Then she picks up her phone and answers Garrett's text with one word. No.

Prepare a negotiation on interests, not positions: know both sides' alternatives, find the zone where an agreement beats both, and bring an objective standard. A bluff about an alternative is dishonest, and it's also bad preparation.

Wednesday, December 14. Pueblo. They drove down I-25 in the dark and got there early. Aldergrove's plant was a long brick building on the south side with a newer metal one bolted to its end, and the conference room was upstairs in the old part, with a window that looked straight across the road at the steel mill: a long brown shed with steam rising from one end, rail cars stacked with pipe, and a crane that never seemed to move until you looked away and back.

Aldergrove's president was a big quiet man in his sixties with a notebook he didn't open. Their lawyer was a woman with a laptop she did. Nell, who'd written the letter, sat at the end of the table nearest the window with a folder in front of her and the old steel badge on its lanyard that Sam had noticed in April.

Peg opened with interests, theirs and Tallgrass's, in that order, and asked whether she'd got Aldergrove's right. The president corrected one of them and added another. For forty minutes it went the way the yellow pad had said it might.

At 10:30 Peg's phone lit up and she put Garrett on speaker, as agreed, for his check in. He listened for about a minute. Then he said, in the warm voice he used on investors: Let me be clear, folks. Tallgrass has options. Kestrel can have a valve in Watkins by May. If Aldergrove wants to play claims, we can play contracts.
Nobody said anything. Aldergrove's lawyer started typing. The president closed his notebook, which he hadn't opened. Nell turned and looked out of the window at the mill.

Let's take fifteen minutes, Peg says, and the president nods like a man who's done this before. In the hall by a vending machine Sam takes the phone off speaker. They need to know we're not soft. They know what we can do, sir, Sam says. They also know the valve's already in the stage and Kestrel can't do May. Every time somebody from our side says it, they hear 2035. Peg, beside him, says nothing, on purpose. You signed Peg's limits on Monday. Either they hold, or I drive home and you come down here yourself. A long silence on the line. They hold. Take me off the dial in. Back in the room Peg says one sentence. Mr. Lyle wanted you to know how seriously Tallgrass takes this. I speak for Tallgrass today. The president opens his notebook.
When your own side's conflict surfaces in front of the other party, take it offline. Assess it, approach the person directly and privately, settle who has authority, and come back with one voice.

During the recess Nell didn't go for coffee. She stood at the window with her arms folded and looked at the mill, and after a minute Sam went and stood beside her, because it seemed she'd wanted somebody to.

My father used to bring me up here on Saturdays when I was a kid, she said. This was his office, before it was a conference room. He liked to watch the mill. He said it was the only thing in Pueblo that worked harder than he did. She turned the steel badge on its lanyard so he could read it. It wasn't her name. E. GARRITY. PRESIDENT. Emmett. He'd have told you to call him Em. Nobody did after 2035.

The agency terminated us for default in September of 2035. Every contract we had with them, the same week. We had four hundred and ten people. By 2037 we had sixty one. It took an appeals board four years to say we hadn't been in default, that the valve met everything the contract asked of it. They changed it to a termination for convenience and paid us our costs, and nobody put that in the paper. By then it was 2039 and he was the man who'd killed the Petrel, in every bar on this side of town.

He wrote to the investigation board every June twelfth. One page, and that page you've got, the copy clipped to it. We're still asking about cycle three. W was Wendell Price. You've worked that out. My father meant to call him in 2034 and didn't, because by then Wendell was the agency's man, and you didn't call the agency's people. Nobody ever wrote back.

She looked at the end of the table, where Aldergrove's president had left his notebook. He died at his desk in March of 2041. That desk, they kept it. His heart, the doctor said. He was sixty three. He'd already written that year's letter. It was in the drawer with the copy clipped to it, and I mailed it in June, and I've mailed one every June since, to whoever has the Mars work. This year it's you. I didn't want to wait till June.

So you should know why I wrote the claim. We need the money. We're sixty people. That's real, and it's not why. The Petrel killed my father, Mr. Okafor. It took six years to do it. I won't ship a valve I don't trust, for a fixed price or for anything else, and I'd rather be fired than be asked to. A breath. I'd rather you didn't fire me.

They went back to the table. Aldergrove's president restated it plainly: $1,008,000 for the past hours, and the task order for the rest. Peg had her pad face down in front of her. Garrett's signed limit on the past hours was $1.0 million. The program's own work orders came to $864,000.

Peg turns the pad over and walks the president through the work orders, one by one. The six hundred archive hours were Aldergrove's choice, and he says so before she has to. They shake on $864,000 at a quarter to one. The task order goes as drafted: target cost $4.0 million, eight percent target fee, 80/20, the fee floor and cap, the monthly data package, and every finding shared with the readiness board with Aldergrove credited by name. Nell asks for one thing more, and Peg writes it into the statement of work in her own words before anyone can argue: Deliverable 1: an answer to the question Aldergrove has asked every June since 2036 about cycle 3 after a cold soak, or a written statement of why there isn't one yet. Nell reads it twice. He'd have liked that, she says. He'd have said it was badly punctuated.

Monday, December 19. The settlement had come to $864,000, and the new task order had a target price of its own. In June the program had set aside money inside its contingency for AR 2207's future costs, Aldergrove's support among them. Quinn had it all on one page with the gap circled: about $3.3 million more than the June line.

Garrett had a suggestion, which he made in the hallway, which was where he made the suggestions he didn't want minuted. The Breather fabrication account has room this quarter. Charge it there. The valve line won't show a thing.

At 11 Calvin Osterhout, the ARA's comptroller, called from Washington. He'd seen the board's notice of a new cost type task order and he had two questions, which he asked in the order he cared about them. Where's the money coming from? And does the number I give the partners move?

The program's estimate at completion was $2.6 billion, the number the Rule 4.2 notice had carried since July, against the $2.4 billion baseline, or $2.472 billion with the management reserve on top. The partners were still taking up the October quarterly.

Quinn moves the money on Tuesday and writes down where it came from: the settlement and the task order's target price, out of contingency, against the AR 2207 line and then the general pool for the rest. She works the estimate at completion again. The July bottom up had carried an allowance for most of it, so the bottom up stays about 2,600, and she shows the Aldergrove line on its own row so anyone can see it. She adds the one thing a cost type contract changes: there's no ceiling, so the estimate has a range, and she shows it. Sam calls Calvin back at four with all of it. There's a pause on the line. All right. I'll fight you on the next one anyway.

Pay for an identified risk from the contingency held for it, record the draw, update the forecast, and report it through governance with the source. Management reserve waits for what nobody saw coming.

Sunday, December 25. Christmas. Sam hadn't put up a tree. He'd hung Grace's red glass pepper on the knob of the cabinet over the coffee maker, where Ada would have put it at the very top, and at eight he sat at the kitchen table and recorded a log, and watched it back, and it was the voice the whole way through, cheerful, every sentence. He didn't send it. The last time he'd seen her without a screen between them was at the crew bus at the Cape, in the dark, in December of 2058. She'd said she'd log every week. He'd said, Your mother would never have let you go. She'd looked at him for a second, and then she'd got on the bus. She'd logged every week since. Neither of them had brought it up. On Friday he sent a short one about Pueblo instead.
Tuesday, January 3, 2062. 5:40 AM. The two note chime.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3866. One way, 16 minutes 53 seconds. Margin, 602 days. Hi, Dad. Log one. I'm numbering them now. Comms says that in the weeks around conjunction some packets don't get through, and the ones that do come in out of order. So from now on every log has a number, and if you get eleven and then thirteen, you'll know there was a twelve, and you'll know I sent it. You'll want to fill it in. Don't. Just know it was there. Christmas was good. We had one. Bay A made a tree out of a trellis and forty empty seed packets on strings, and Malik climbed it to put a star on top, which was a sample tube with foil on it, and he only coughed twice, and medical found two of the good inhalers in a kit from '57 behind a panel nobody had opened in years, and gave him one, and he carries it around like a medal. You didn't send one for Christmas. That's okay. I think you recorded one. You always record one and then sit there deciding, and I can see you deciding from here, which is three hundred million kilometers, I looked it up. Your Friday one was short. You said Pueblo four times. You didn't say anything about the valve lady except that she has a view of a steel mill, so something happened, and it's hers, and okay. Now the thing. I should have told you this a long time ago, and I didn't, because I thought it was the kind of thing a director tells his agency and not the kind of thing a daughter tells her dad. The spare stacks are gone. All six. Hollis's weekly says six RP-55 stacks in stores. They're not in stores. They're in the plant. The first one went in more than a year ago. The last one went in three weeks before you got the ship. Every time one of the old stacks quit, we put a spare in, and the stores list never changed, because taking a stack off it is a form, and the form goes to Earth, and nobody wanted to be the one who sent it. So it's still on the page every Monday. Six spares. There's nothing on the shelf, Dad. I went and looked. There's a shelf. My number has always been the plant with all six already in it. The agency's model puts them in this year. That's most of your sixty days. I'm sorry I didn't say. I thought it was his to say. He hasn't, and I don't think he's going to, and the people building the thing that's supposed to replace this plant should know the old one has nothing left in its pockets. I watched yours twice. You looked tired. You only look tired when you're telling me everything. 602. Same minus nine. Love you. Log one. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on the shelf, and on her hand against it.

At 7:10 he put one question into the morning packet for the joint Breather team, the routine way, as part of the cutover inventory the plan needed anyway: Q2: Station stores count of RP-55 stacks, by serial. The answer came back the next morning, at the end of the station's shift, from Chiamaka Okonkwo, who led Breather operations on the station and answered exactly what she was asked.

Chiamaka's answers, sol 3867. Question two, understood as how many RP-55 stacks are in station stores, by serial. Answer: none. All six are installed in the plant, with the plant log references attached, and the stores list was never updated; a correction has gone to the director to sign. Question three, from the station: does the cutover plan assume spares from stores, and if it does, who decides what replaces them?
The packet went where all the packets went, to the joint team and to the ARA's mission assurance office, which read every one.

It did assume them. Quinn found the line in the cutover plan in four minutes: during the forty sols it would take to install and start the Breather, the old plant would keep the station breathing, and if one of its stacks quit, the station would put in a spare from stores. The risk register said the same thing in different words. So did the ARA's own margin model, which credited six spares going into the plant in 2062. Behind all of it sat the fourteen days of declared reserve at the end of the window, which had assumed the old plant could stretch. Even the dashed OPTION diamond on Quinn's plan had a footnote that began, if the station's spares hold.

It takes two days. Quinn rewrites the cutover plan around six bridge stacks flown on Halcyon. Hana weighs them, 430 kilograms with mounts, against the cargo module's margin and the propellant behind it, and it fits, with less left over than she likes. The risk register's response for a stack failure during cutover changes from station spares to VOID, in capitals, and a new risk takes its place. Peg starts a procurement file. The funding goes to the ARA as a change request, because the stacks are station property replacing the station's own spares. And Sam writes to the board's clerk and Hale's office about the margin, citing Chiamaka's packet and the plant log, and nothing else: the ARA's model credits six spare stacks that were installed in 2060, and the board may want to check it. Hale calls at six. Sixty days? About that, ma'am. The board should check it. Not me. She's quiet for a while. Then the board will have it by Friday.

A new fact that touches several plans is an integration problem. Assess it across the integrated plan, update the subsidiary plans and the risk register together, and report what governance needs to know through the right channel, from the record.
Monday, January 9. One way or another, the program had to buy six RP-55 stacks, and they had to be in Watkins by May 15 to make the cargo module's manifest closeout on June 1.

Rio Puerco had built the station's plant in 2055. Paloma Benavidez, their test engineer, called from Albuquerque at eight with her safety glasses on her head and a stack of old binders behind her. I ran RP-55 acceptance my first year here. I was twenty eight. The tooling's in the back of Building 3 under a tarp with my handwriting on it. Rio Puerco's offer was an incentive contract: target cost $12.0 million, target fee $1.2 million, target price $13.2 million, share 80/20, ceiling $14.4 million. Or a firm fixed price of $15.1 million, which Paloma said, without being asked, was the same work with the line's restart risk priced in.

Garrett wanted to build them at Watkins. We've got a stack assembly line. It's paid for. We keep the capability. Quinn had the numbers for that too. Restarting an RP-55 line at Tallgrass meant new tooling, a requalification of a design nobody there had touched, and training: $5.0 million fixed, then about $1.6 million a stack. And Tallgrass's stack assembly line was the Breather's critical path, which it had been since March.

Quinn does the comparison in front of everybody. Making six costs $5.0 million plus $9.6 million, $14.6 million, and takes the Breather's critical path to do it. Buying at target costs $13.2 million, and even at the ceiling, $14.4 million, it's cheaper than making. The line Garrett says is paid for is paid for either way. Peg checks the share and the ceiling, works out where Rio Puerco stops sharing, and writes it on the file as a number to watch. The contract is signed on Wednesday. Paloma sends a photo that afternoon of a tarp coming off a machine. Hi.

A make or buy decision compares the full cost of each option over the quantity you need, leaves sunk costs out, and weighs capacity, expertise, and schedule. For a defined product with some cost risk, an incentive contract with a ceiling shares the risk and caps it.

Wednesday, February 8. Hana came to the change board with a proposal from the root cause team. The seat insert in the 7740 was a fluoropolymer, and two lots of it from 2058 had come from different batches of raw material. Nobody had ever compared them cold. Aldergrove's engineers wanted a materials lab to do it: six weeks and about $600,000.
Under the incentive fee task order, every dollar of it would be an allowable cost. The target cost had been $4.0 million since December.

Aldergrove's engineers had already asked the lab for a sample shipping kit. Garrett, at the end of the table, didn't see a problem. It's cost plus. Tell them to do it. That's the whole point of cost plus.
Hana looked at Sam. She'd been looking at him that way all week, as if she was about to say something else, and then not saying it.

CR-0401 goes up the same afternoon: the study, its cost, its six weeks inside the root cause plan, what it might find, what it changes in the risk register. The board approves it. On Thursday Peg signs modification 2, raising the target cost to $4.6 million and the target fee with it, and leaving the fee floor and cap where they were, so the incentive still measures what it was built to measure. Quinn updates the plan. Aldergrove ships the samples on Friday. Nell sends Peg one line, copied to Sam. That's the first time in twenty six years anybody's changed a contract with us before the work instead of after.

Contract change control runs alongside the project's: assess the change at the board, then let the person with contracting authority modify the contract and adjust its terms, and update the plan, before the work begins.
Monday, February 13. Page eight came in the mail on a cold clear afternoon, green ink, Golden postmark. Sam read it at the kitchen table with the butter knife beside it and his coat still on.
Oh eight ten. CALLED GARRITY BACK. TOLD HIM WE NEED IT ON THE 30TH. HE ASKED IF I'D LOOKED AT HIS ROW 3. TOLD HIM I'D LOOKED AT THE SCHEDULE.

He read the eight ten line four times, and the eight eleven line under it, THAT WAS TRUE, until it stopped being words. Then the line for April 30 at half past two. Filed the letter with the receiving papers. He'd sat across a table from Nell in her father's old office in December, and she'd told him about the drawer, and here was the other drawer.

The task order's first deliverable had her father's question in it, in Peg's words, badly punctuated. Nell had started calling Sam on Thursday afternoons, not about anything in particular, to tell him what the cold data said that week. Most weeks it said nothing yet. She called anyway.

The change board's minutes for December 7 had one line nobody had argued with: a member of Tallgrass's investor board chairs Kestrel Flow Controls, so any decision involving Kestrel comes to the board without Garrett's vote. Garrett had initialed it himself.

The board's clerk had acknowledged his note about the spare stacks in capitals and put the ARA's margin model on the March agenda. Sixty days of somebody's number would be argued about by people with badges, in public, which was where it belonged.

In Albuquerque the RP-55 line had made its first stack on February 6. Paloma had sent a photograph with her hand on the housing for scale. Rio Puerco's estimate at completion was 12.3 million, comfortably under the 13.5 million Peg had written on the file.

He made a list in the notebook of what had gone right since November, because Ray had told him once that a man who only lists his mistakes stops being able to see the rest. It was longer than he'd expected. He didn't trust it much.

Then he took the photocopy out of his briefcase, the one with STILL ASKING beside the third row, and put it in an envelope, and wrote Ruth's address in Golden on the front. He didn't seal it. He put it on the counter by the door, under his keys, where he'd see it every morning.

Friday, February 17. At 6:40 PM Hana Iwasaki was at his office door with her coat on and her car keys in her hand. She'd been there for a while before he looked up; he could tell from the way she was standing.
Can you come out to the stand? she said. Tonight. Just you. There's something I have to tell you, and I want to tell you out there.
He got his coat. On the way out they passed under the countdown clock, 366, and in the morning it would say 365. A year, exactly, and the wind coming up off the plains in the dark.
